title: Overestimation bias & sample efficiency
blurb: Why max over noisy estimates is optimistic, and what to do

hook.title: Taking the best of noisy quotes
hook.text: You ask three contractors to quote a job whose true price is **zero** (free). Their quotes are noisy: +0.5, +0.2, −0.3. If you always take the most *favourable-looking* one for planning, you consistently believe in a bonus that isn't there. A Q-network's value estimates are noisy too; the **max** in the Bellman target systematically picks up positive noise, and since the new estimates are trained *toward* these inflated targets, the optimism feeds on itself.
hook.recall: Remember the noisy quotes: $\max$ over noisy estimates is biased upward, so targets are too high and the error compounds. Real-world data is expensive, so sample efficiency matters; TD3, SAC, Maxmin Q-learning and REDQ address estimation bias.

explore.intro: True $Q^*=0$ for every action; the estimates are noisy. How big is the error of $\max_aQ_\varphi$?
tasks: Raise the number of actions with $\sigma=0.4$. What happens to the bias?
Turn on the independent-evaluation toggle (an extra idea).
explore.takeaway: $\mathbb E[\max_a\hat Q]\ge\max_a\mathbb E[\hat Q]$: noise makes the max optimistic. The slide lists TD3, SAC, Maxmin Q-learning and REDQ as fixes.

build.prompt: True $Q^*(s,a_i)=0$ for all actions, but the network outputs $0.5,\,0.2,\,-0.3$. With $r=0$, the Bellman target uses $\max_{a'}Q_\varphi(s,a')$. **Predict**: compared with the true value 0, the target is…
build.reveal: The max picks $0.5$, so $y=\gamma\cdot0.5>0$ although the true value is 0. Training $Q_\varphi(s,a)$ toward that target pushes its value up, making the overestimate worse.

questions.prompt: Using the slide’s noisy values $(0.5,0.2,-0.3)$, $r=0$ and $\gamma=0.9$, what is the Bellman target $y=r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q_\varphi$?
What will the update tend to do to $Q_\varphi(s,a)$ in that situation?
options: Push it up toward the inflated target
questions.explanation: Targets above truth drag estimates upward.

questions.prompt: Why is sample efficiency important according to the slides?
options: Collecting data points in real-world applications is expensive; wall-clock time is not the same as efficiency
questions.explanation: Each real-world sample can cost money or time.

options: TD3 addresses function approximation error in actor–critic methods
SAC and Maxmin Q-learning are listed as ways to fix estimation problems
REDQ is a randomised ensembled double Q-learning method
The slide lists TD3, SAC, Maxmin Q-learning and REDQ as ways to create overestimation bias
questions.explanation: They are listed as ways to *fix* it.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm family lists SAC as an example?
questions.explanation: Policy gradients: REINFORCE; value-based: DQN; actor–critic: DDPG, Soft Actor-Critic; model-based: Dyna.

questions.prompt: *“Q-estimate noise has mean zero, so $\mathbb E[\max_a\hat Q]=\max_aQ^*$: no overestimation can occur.”* What’s wrong?
options: The max of noisy values is biased upward: $\mathbb E[\max\hat Q]\ge\max\mathbb E[\hat Q]$ (try the explorer); zero-mean noise doesn’t cancel inside a max
questions.explanation: The best-looking quote is selected *because* it is lucky.
